sentences.text: Nikolai Braun had done the asking for forty-one years and he was not going to be doing it a forty-second.
He had had a stroke in the September.
He was alive and he was at home and he was, by all accounts, entirely himself in the head, and he could not walk to the end of the lane, let alone up the scree.

The valley discussed the problem for most of October in the way that valley discussed everything, which was by not discussing it in front of children and then discussing it at length in front of children who were pretending to read.
Lise, who was twelve, learned the following.
That the asking was not a ceremony.
There were no words.
Nobody wore anything.
If you went up there expecting to say a formula, Nikolai had told the last three people who asked him, you would come down again with nothing having happened and you would feel extremely silly.
That you went alone, and in the last week of February or the first of March, and you went up to wherever she was, and you asked, and either she put it down or she did not.
That it had not always been Nikolai.
Before him it had been a woman called Frau Ebner for a very long time, and before her a man whose name was on the war memorial, and before that the records got vague.
And that in 1934, and again in 1968, the person who went up had come back down without it, and both of those springs had come in the second week of May and both of those years had been hard.
1968 was in living memory when Lise was small.

Frau Hofer, who was ninety and who had been a young woman that year, would talk about it if you got her going: the hay running out in March, the road shut until the twenty-first of April, the two families who left the valley that summer and did not come back.

She never once said who had gone up that year and failed, and nobody else ever said it either, and Lise worked out at about ten that this was deliberate and that the name was known to everyone over sixty.
What nobody could tell Lise, because nobody knew, was what *properly* meant.
She asked her mother, who said she supposed it meant being sincere.
She asked Herr Vogel at the shop, who said it meant you had to mean it, which was the same answer with fewer syllables.
She asked Nikolai Braun himself, in the front room of his house, in November, with his daughter listening from the kitchen and pretending not to.
He took a long time to get the sentence out.
That was one of the things the stroke had left him.
He said: "It means you have to know what you're asking for." Lise said that everybody knew what they were asking for.
They were asking for spring.
And Nikolai Braun laughed, which was alarming, and then took another long time, and said: "That's what I said in 1962.
And I came down that day and it was still there in her mouth and I was up that mountain three more times before the ninth of March."
